clinicalPearls: Group A Streptococcus (GAS; S. pyogenes) is the only common cause of sore throat that should be treated with antibiotics; GAS accounts for 20-40% of exudative pharyngitis in children and is rare under age 3 (p.1208).

Streptococcal pharyngitis cannot be reliably diagnosed on clinical grounds alone given overlap with many viral and bacterial causes; throat culture remains the diagnostic gold standard, with rapid antigen tests (specificity >95%) a useful adjunct (p.1208).
Antibiotic treatment of GAS pharyngitis is given primarily to prevent suppurative complications and acute rheumatic fever; symptoms resolve in 3-5 days and are shortened little by treatment (p.1208).
Prevention of ARF depends on eradicating the organism from the pharynx (not just symptom resolution) and requires a 10-day penicillin course; a single dose or short course is inadequate (p.1208).
Penicillin treatment of streptococcal pharyngitis reduces the likelihood of ARF but NOT of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis (p.1209).

Worldwide, GAS infections and their post-infectious sequelae (chiefly ARF and rheumatic heart disease) cause an estimated 500,000 deaths/year; incidence of GAS disease and RHD is roughly tenfold higher in resource-limited countries (p.1206-1207).

Scarlet fever is streptococcal infection (usually pharyngitis) plus a rash from pyrogenic exotoxins: blanching sandpaper-textured papular rash on trunk and extremities sparing palms and soles, with circumoral pallor, strawberry tongue, and Pastia's lines in skin folds, followed by desquamation of palms and soles (p.1209).

Impetigo is most often a superficial GAS infection (occasionally other streptococci or S. aureus) of young children; honey/amber crusted lesions on face and legs; lesions are generally NOT painful and fever is NOT a feature — if fever is present, suspect deeper infection or another diagnosis (p.1209-1210).

Erysipelas is a streptococcal cellulitis of the superficial dermis: bright red, warm, shiny, edematous plaque with a sharply demarcated raised border and peau d'orange texture, typically on the face (malar) or lower extremities, with abrupt onset, fever and chills; classic cases are almost always due to beta-hemolytic streptococci (usually GAS) (p.1210).

Streptococcal cellulitis favors sites of disrupted lymphatic drainage (prior cellulitis, post-mastectomy/axillary dissection arm, prior DVT or lymphedema leg, saphenous vein harvest site); treating tinea pedis can stop recurrent leg cellulitis after vein harvest (p.1210-1211).
GAS is among the few pathogens producing wound infection and surrounding cellulitis within the first 24 h after surgery, with thin exudate and rapid spread (p.1211).

Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: GAS is implicated in ~60% of cases; early surgical exploration and extensive debridement are diagnostic, therapeutic, and life-saving, with antibiotics as a critical adjunct (p.1211).

Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS) features fever, hypotension, renal impairment, and respiratory distress; in contrast to staphylococcal TSS, most patients with streptococcal TSS are bacteremic, rash usually does NOT develop, and the most common associated infection is a soft tissue infection (necrotizing fasciitis, myositis, or cellulitis) (p.1211-1212).
Streptococcal TSS carries a mortality rate of >=30%, mostly from shock and respiratory failure; because of its rapidly progressive lethal course, early recognition is essential (p.1212).

Group B Streptococcus (GBS; S. agalactiae) is a leading cause of neonatal sepsis and meningitis and of peripartum fever; early-onset disease (first week, median 20 h) is acquired from the colonized maternal genital tract, while late-onset disease (1 week-3 months) most often presents as meningitis, frequently capsular type III (p.1212-1213).

GBS infection in adults increasingly affects the elderly and those with chronic illness (e.g., diabetes, malignancy), presenting as cellulitis/soft-tissue infection including diabetic ulcers, UTI, pneumonia, endocarditis, and septic arthritis (p.1213-1214).
harrison.pathophysiology: GAS (S. pyogenes) is the single species of Lancefield group A, a beta-hemolytic, chain-forming, gram-positive facultative anaerobe. M protein (encoded by the emm gene, >200 emm types) is the major surface protein and chief virulence factor: it resists phagocytic killing partly by binding plasma fibrinogen and interfering with complement deposition, and type-specific anti-M antibody confers protection only against the same M type. A hyaluronic acid capsule (a weak immunogen owing to structural identity with mammalian connective tissue) protects against phagocytosis and aids pharyngeal colonization via CD44 binding; capsule is not essential for virulence. GAS elaborates streptolysins S and O, streptokinase, DNases, SpyCEP (cleaves IL-8 to impair neutrophil recruitment), and pyrogenic exotoxins (formerly erythrogenic toxins) that cause the scarlet fever rash and act as superantigens triggering T-cell cytokine release, implicated in severe invasive disease including necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal TSS. The post-infectious sequelae ARF (uniquely associated with S. pyogenes) and PSGN are thought to result from immune responses to streptococcal infection. GBS is encapsulated by 1 of 10 polysaccharides; the capsule is a key virulence factor and type-specific anticapsular antibody is protective.
additionalDifferentials: Scarlet fever differential: measles and other viral exanthems, Kawasaki disease, toxic shock syndrome, and systemic allergic/drug eruptions (p.1209)

Pharyngitis differential includes group C/G streptococci, mixed anaerobes (Vincent's angina), Arcanobacterium haemolyticum, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Corynebacterium diphtheriae, EBV/CMV/HIV, and other viruses (Table 153-2, p.1208)
Impetigo differential: bullous impetigo due to S. aureus, and herpetic lesions (orolabial HSV, chickenpox, or zoster), distinguished by grouped discrete vesicles and positive Tzanck/PCR (p.1210)
infectionMimics: Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis/soft tissue infection mimicking streptococcal cellulitis (suspect S. aureus when cellulitis develops around a wound or ulcer) (p.1210-1211)
Bullous impetigo (S. aureus) mimicking streptococcal impetigo (p.1210)
Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (shares features with streptococcal TSS, but staph TSS patients are usually not bacteremic) (p.1211-1212)
Herpes simplex virus or varicella-zoster lesions mimicking impetigo (p.1210)
nonInfectiousMimics: Systemic allergic reactions / drug eruptions (mimic scarlet fever) (p.1209)
additionalInvestigations: Throat culture (gold standard; vigorous rubbing of both tonsillar pillars) and rapid antigen test (latex agglutination/EIA, specificity >95%, relative sensitivity 70-90%); confirm negative rapid test with culture in higher-risk individuals (p.1208)
Antibody tests to streptolysin O (ASO) and DNase B for serodiagnosis of preceding streptococcal infection in suspected ARF or PSGN (p.1207)
emm-typing by PCR/sequencing of the variable region of the emm gene (CDC database) for strain typing (p.1207)
In streptococcal TSS, laboratory findings: marked left shift with immature granulocytes, hypocalcemia, hypoalbuminemia, and thrombocytopenia (worsening on day 2-3) (p.1211)
Blood cultures (most streptococcal TSS patients are bacteremic) (p.1211-1212)
Early surgical exploration of suspected necrotizing fasciitis for diagnosis (reveals fascial-plane necrosis and inflammatory fluid without muscle involvement) (p.1211)
Cultures of vesicular fluid in difficult impetigo cases; culture to rule out MRSA if empirical treatment fails (p.1210)
redFlags: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency: severe pain out of proportion to physical findings, with only minimal early skin erythema; progression over hours to dusky/mottled erythema and edema; tenderness evolving into anesthesia from infarction of cutaneous nerves — demands early surgical exploration and debridement (p.1211)
Streptococcal TSS: rapidly progressive, lethal (mortality >=30%) with hypotension and multiorgan failure; early recognition essential (p.1211-1212)
Fever in a patient with impetigo suggests extension to deeper tissues or an alternative diagnosis (p.1210)
GAS bacteremia without an identified source raises the possibility of endocarditis, occult abscess, or osteomyelitis (p.1212)
Unusually severe or prolonged pharyngitis, or localized pain with high fever and toxic appearance, suggests a peritonsillar or parapharyngeal abscess (p.1209)
harrison.prognosis: Uncomplicated GAS pharyngitis is self-limited, with symptoms resolving in 3-5 days. Suppurative complications (peritonsillar/retropharyngeal abscess, cervical lymphadenitis, sinusitis, otitis, meningitis, bacteremia, endocarditis, pneumonia) are now uncommon with antibiotics; nonsuppurative sequelae are ARF and PSGN. Necrotizing fasciitis and streptococcal TSS are rapidly progressive and life-threatening; streptococcal TSS has a mortality rate of >=30%. Globally GAS sequelae account for ~500,000 deaths/year. Neonatal GBS incidence has fallen from ~2-3 to ~0.6 per 1000 live births with prenatal screening. Recurrent invasive GBS in adults occurs in ~4% of cases.
pitfalls: Diagnosing streptococcal pharyngitis on clinical grounds alone is unreliable; clinicians over-prescribe antibiotics for sore throat (p.1208)
Rapid antigen tests are less sensitive than culture (relative sensitivity 70-90%), so a negative rapid test should be confirmed by throat culture in higher-risk patients (p.1208)
Improper swab technique lowers rapid-test sensitivity; both tonsillar pillars (and any exudate/ulceration) must be vigorously sampled (p.1208)
In necrotizing fasciitis, early physical findings may be unimpressive despite severe pain; relying on skin appearance delays diagnosis (p.1211)
Macrolide resistance is common in many countries and rising in invasive US GAS isolates (>30% since 2021); avoid macrolides where resistance exceeds 5-10% unless susceptibility is known (p.1208-1209)
Clindamycin resistance occurs in >=30% of invasive GAS isolates; susceptibility should not be assumed without in vitro testing before relying on clindamycin (p.1212)

Aggressive eradication of asymptomatic GAS pharyngeal carriage is usually not justified (carriers have lower risk of ARF and of transmission than symptomatic patients); exceptions arise when a carrier is a source of transmission to others (p.1209)

Endocarditis due to nonenterococcal group D streptococci (S. gallolyticus/S. bovis group) is associated with occult GI neoplasm (often colon carcinoma/polyp; abnormalities in >60%) and should prompt GI evaluation (p.1214)
harrison.severityClassification: Streptococcal toxic shock syndrome case definition (CDC, 1993; updated 2010; Table 153-4): I. Isolation of GAS from (A) a normally sterile site or (B) a nonsterile site; II. Clinical signs of severity = (A) hypotension AND (B) >=2 of: renal impairment, coagulopathy, liver function impairment, ARDS, generalized erythematous macular rash that may desquamate, or soft tissue necrosis (including necrotizing fasciitis or myositis) or gangrene. A DEFINITE case meets IA + IIA + IIB; a PROBABLE case meets IB + IIA + IIB if no other etiology is identified. Pharyngitis pretest risk is stratified clinically by the Centor criteria (fever history, absence of cough, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, tonsillar exudate/swelling).
references: Wessels MR. Streptococcal Infections. In: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22nd ed, Ch. 153, pp. 1206-1214.
Carapetis JR et al. The global burden of group A streptococcal diseases. Lancet Infect Dis 5:685, 2005.
Streptococcal Toxic Shock Syndrome (STSS) 2010 Case Definition, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
management: Penicillin, or amoxicillin, as first-line antibiotic for group A streptococcal pharyngitis, completing the full course to eradicate pharyngeal carriage and prevent acute rheumatic fever
A macrolide or first-generation cephalosporin for penicillin-allergic patients
For invasive disease and streptococcal toxic shock syndrome, combine a beta-lactam with clindamycin to suppress toxin production
Adjunctive intravenous immunoglobulin for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome
Urgent surgical exploration and debridement for necrotising fasciitis
Supportive intensive care with fluid resuscitation and organ support for invasive and toxic-shock disease
Drainage of suppurative complications such as peritonsillar abscess, and secondary antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever
